extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars interested in Latin American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Identify the stylistic, thematic, historical, and publishing features that define (or are commonly used to evaluate) novels and writers associated with the Latin American Boom of the 1960s–70s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernist/technical complexity (nonlinear time and multiple perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boom novels are essentially modernist novels. They treat time as nonlinear, often use more than one perspective or narrative voice and feature a great number of neologisms (the coining of new words or phrases), puns and even profanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pope: 'It relied on a Cubist superposition of different points of view, it made time and lineal progress questionable, and it was technically complex.' Examples: complex chronology and multiple voices as in works by Cortázar, Fuentes, Vargas Llosa and García Márquez.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic innovation and use of vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistically self-assured writing that uses the vernacular without apologies; frequent neologisms, puns, and bold lexical experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic features include coining new words, playful language, and incorporation of everyday speech. The page cites the Boom's 'linguistic sophistication' and use of vernacular as a hallmark; Cortázar and other authors exemplify radical experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing fantastical and mundane (magical realism / lo real maravilloso)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaks down the barriers between the fantastical and the mundane, transforming this mixture into a new reality; unreal things are treated as if realistic and mundane things as if unreal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a 'key aesthetic mode' and illustrated by García Márquez (e.g., the ascending woman in One Hundred Years of Solitude). References Carpentier's 'lo real maravilloso' and defines plots that combine the true, imaginary and nonexistent, making them difficult to separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in history and the dictator novel (historical fiction linked to contemporary politics)
rubrics_metrics.description: An engagement with history, often via the 'dictator novel' that portrays historical figures/events to draw clear connections to contemporary Latin American politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Roa Bastos's I, the Supreme depicts a 19th-century Paraguayan dictatorship while speaking to the context of Alfredo Stroessner's regime. Boom novelists depict parallel and alternative histories and participate in cultural/political debates questioning the meaning of history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement and topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are often explicitly political or shaped by the political climate of the 1960s–70s (Cuban Revolution, Cold War, authoritarian regimes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes many writers advocated political and social action; political events (Cuban Revolution, coups, Operation Condor) formed the background for much writing. Examples include Libro de Manuel (explicitly political) and public stances by authors like Cortázar and García Márquez.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internationalism and questioning of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on both historical and political internationalism, questioning regional and national identity, and awareness of hemisphereic and worldwide economic and ideological issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hallmarks include treatment of rural and urban settings, international concerns, and polemicism/timeliness. Boom novels often address identity beyond national borders and engage global ideological questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement via nonlinearity (active deciphering required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronological intricacy and narrative looseness make the reader an active participant in deciphering the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states that in the 1960s language 'loosen[s] up' and chronology becomes intricate, making the reader active. Cortázar's Hopscotch (155 chapters with optional orders) is an explicit example of structural strategies that demand reader participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metafiction and reflexivity (fiction on fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Later Boom work often turns to reflection on its own writing — metafictional techniques and self-referentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late-period writers increasingly produced fiction that reflects on the act and status of writing itself, showing characters and story lines that interrogate narrative construction and the postmodern condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental formal devices (e.g., modular/optional chapters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Radical experimentation with form and structure, such as expendable chapters, alternative reading orders, and formally disruptive layouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cortázar's Hopscotch is cited: 155 chapters, 99 of which are 'expendable' and can be read in multiple orders. I, the Supreme has been compared to Joyce's Ulysses for formal ambition. Formal innovation is a defining production criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing, translation and market access as determinants of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boom's international success depended heavily on publication in European markets, translations, and promotion by publishers/agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seix Barral in Barcelona and figures like Carmen Balcells ('super-agent') were crucial. The page notes that having work published and translated in Europe and beyond helped Latin American novelists reach wider audiences and gain world fame — a procedural/market criterion for impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precursor and influence lineage (Modernism and Vanguardia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationship to European Modernism and Latin American Vanguardia is a criterion for situating Boom works; the movement owes stylistic innovation to both influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists influences (Proust, Joyce, Mann, Sartre, José Martí, Rubén Darío, etc.) and argues Vanguardia writers were 'true precursors.' Evaluating Boom work often involves tracing these literary lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common critical objections (elitism, gender bias, detachment from realities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques used to evaluate or reject Boom works include that they are too experimental and elitist, emphasize masculinity, and can be removed from the political realities they claim to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donald L. Shaw and Mario Benedetti cited criticisms: Boom writers 'represent a privileged class' unrepresentative of average people; the movement's male dominance and treatment of female characters are frequent criticisms. Also, formal experimentation becoming standardized into new stereotypes is noted as an anti-pattern.
